Clarke Schmidt Injury: May be shut down
Schmidt could be shut down for the season if he's unable to pitch Thursday, MLB.com reports.
After completing his recovery from an internal brace procedure he underwent in July of 2025, Schmidt returned to the Yankees and pitched a scoreless two-thirds of an inning against Minnesota on Sept. 16. However, he suffered a biceps injury while warming up in the bullpen four days later. The right-hander reportedly had a "better" day Tuesday, but it's still unclear if he'll be able to return before the end of the season. Should Schmidt not be feeling well enough to pitch by Thursday, the Yankees may decide that he's better off being held out of pitching until 2027.

item.content:encoded:
The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while.
“There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days,” the manager said before the Yankees played the division-winning Rays on Wednesday. “Hopefully, we have a lot of options to choose from.”
THE RETURN OF STANTON (AND GRISHAM)?
Giancarlo Stanton, out since April 24 due to three separate calf strains (two right, one left), and Trent Grisham, sidelined by his second right hamstring strain of the season, took live at-bats in Somerset on Wednesday. Both ran the bases, and Boone said Stanton homered while getting six or seven at-bats.
“They’re knocking on the door,” Boone said, but he wasn’t sure if Stanton, a decorated postseason performer, could be ready for the Wild Card round.
The manager previously said that Grisham could be in play, though he wasn’t expected to be activated before the final five games of the regular season.
Asked what he would need to see from Stanton after a five-month layoff, Boone earnestly said, “I’m not sure.”
“I don’t know that answer,” he continued. “Obviously, there’ll be conversations with him. Does he fit on the roster? Is it realistic? All those things, and I can’t answer that right now.”
With the Yankees already log-jammed with first-base/DH types — Stanton can’t play the outfield anymore — Boone added that the former MVP would probably be used as a pinch-hitter, if anything. While not a big role, Stanton’s right-handed bat could be helpful off the bench if the Yankees face the lefty-heavy Red Sox, their likeliest opponent, in the Wild Card round.
Grisham, meanwhile, would give the Yankees an interesting choice in center field with Spencer Jones handling the position in his absence. Jones has outperformed Grisham at the plate, but both are shaky defenders, and the latter has postseason experience that the rookie does not.
LAGRANGE TO DEBUT?
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said of flamethrowing pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange, who threw live batting practice on Wednesday.
But the skipper noted that a lot of “unknown” comes with righty, who has yet to make his major league debut, only recently returned from a shoulder sprain, and has just eight relief appearances under his belt this season. If the Yankees were to use Lagrange and his 100-plus-mph fastball, it would be out of the bullpen.
Asked why the Yankees don’t just promote Lagrange now, Boone said that they still have to cover innings over the last few games of the regular season. They would also have to clear space for him on the 40-man and active rosters.
While Lagrange is 23 and Stanton is 36, both are in similar positions in that they offer the Yankees an intriguing combination of upside, mystery and risk. Asked how Boone might personally weigh all that as the Yankees prepare to make their postseason roster, he said the club will “make the best decision possible” “if those guys are truly pushing into the conversation.”
“Carlos is in the stay ready [phase]. G [got] at-bats today,” Boone said. “All, at least, putting them on the outskirts of the conversation, if nothing else.”
WHO STARTS GAME 1?
Cam Schlittler is the clear frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award. So he’s obviously going to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round, right?
“Not necessarily,” Boone said. “We’ll see. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 doesn’t affect the next series. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 can pitch Game 2 and Game 5 in the next series, for example. We’ll decide what makes the most sense, just matching up how we want to go with it. But Cam would certainly be one of those first two games.”
Gerrit Cole, who totaled two earned runs, three walks and eight strikeouts over 5.2 innings and 105 pitches on Wednesday against the Rays, is currently lined up for Game 1 of the Wild Card round on extra rest. The 2023 Cy Young winner, now 22 starts removed from Tommy John surgery, has struggled to get swing-and-miss this season. He’s also faltered against the Red Sox throughout his career. With Max Fried and Carlos Rodón also in the rotation, the case can be made that Cole has been the Yankees’ fourth-best starter lately.
Schlittler, who dominated Boston in last year’s Wild Card series, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1. He is scheduled to make his final start of the regular season on Thursday.
VOLPE AT THIRD? MCMAHON OFF THE ROSTER?
With the lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon putting the finishing touches on an abysmal offensive season and taking a step back defensively, the righty-hitting Anthony Volpe did some pregame work at third base on Wednesday. Boone expects the shortstop turned second baseman to play the hot corner in one or two games before the regular season ends.
“Good to go,” Volpe, who played a few games at third in the minors this year, said of his comfort level at the position.
Meanwhile, José Caballero, another righty, has already gotten some starts at third over McMahon against right-handed pitching. If Volpe shows that he can handle third, it could increase the odds of the Yankees leaving McMahon off their Wild Card roster.
Boone said that he still sees McMahon as a “top-shelf” defender, but he entered Wednesday’s game with -2 Defensive Runs Saved and one Out Above Average, numbers well below career norms. Couple that with a 73 wRC+, and the $16 million man has not been a quality player, though he did hit a grand slam on Wednesday.
“I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I want him in the game and the ball hit to him in a big spot,” Boone said. “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half and lately getting it going. But through his struggles that he’s had offensively, he’s gotten a lot of big hits for us, too, along the way.”
On the subject of third base, Boone also said that he hasn’t given much thought to Jazz Chisholm Jr. trying the position again. However, he’s not ruling it out.
WHAT ABOUT OTHER INJURED ARMS?
Fernando Cruz made a rather adamant appearance in the Yankees’ clubhouse on Wednesday. The reliever, out with a partially torn UCL, repeatedly said that he refused to “accept” the diagnosis.
“I had real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” said Cruz, who isn’t considering surgery right now. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart, it’s not a partial tear.”
While it seems rather improbable that Cruz will pitch again this season, he said that that is his goal, and Boone didn’t rule out the possibility. The righty threw a touch-and-feel bullpen three days ago, and he plans to throw another bullpen on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Clarke Schmidt felt better playing catch on Wednesday than he did on Tuesday after experiencing some biceps cramping over the weekend. However, if the recently returned Tommy John patient is not a viable option by Thursday, “then we’ll probably go a different way,” Boone said, referring to the Yankees’ postseason roster plans.
Finally, Ryan Weathers isn’t expected to throw live batting practice until sometime during the Wild Card series, so he won’t be an option.
With Weathers ruled out and Schmidt’s status uncertain, it will be interesting to see how the Yankees fill out their Wild Card bullpen. On a related note, Boone said that he sees “no scenario” in which the team carries 13 pitchers for the series. They may not even roster 12, he said with so many balls up in the air.
“It depends who’s available and who’s not,” Boone said.

NEW YORK – Consider it a long shot, but Giancarlo Stanton has entered the Yankees’ playoff conversation.
Down at Somerset, the slugging DH – on the injured list since April 25 – is batting against live pitching and even running the bases.
“I heard G went deep over there,’’ manager Aaron Boone said of Stanton’s “six or seven’’ at-bats Wednesday, with at least one home run.
Boone described both Stanton (calf) and Trent Grisham (hamstring) as “knocking on the door’’ in their Somerset rehab, with the lefty-hitting center fielder also hitting and running the bases.
But are they really in consideration for a Wild Card series roster spot?
“I don’t know. Anything’s possible. We’ll see,’’ Boone said Wednesday at Yankee Stadium, with his club already locked into hosting a best-of-three playoff beginning Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a day after Boone said that the Yankees weren't planning on having Aaron Judge ready for the Wild Card series due to a "moderate'' grade right calf strain, the captain told ESPN that he's planning otherwise.
Judge told reporter Jorge Castillo that he's trying "to get my body ready so I'm ready to go'' by Tuesday.
On Monday, Judge had a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection, limiting his activity.
Judge was asked by ESPN if he expected to be on the first round playoff roster replied: "I don't make the roster. I've got no idea."
Giancarlo Stanton's lengthy absence
It’s been five months since Stanton last appeared in Boone’s lineup, due to three separate calf strains – including his current right calf issue.
Due to Stanton’s DH-only status, and the makeup of the Yanks’ current roster, “you’re looking more in a pinch-hit scenario,’’ Boone said of his potential role.
“We’ll see if that’s even a realistic option,’’ said Boone. “I don’t know yet.’’
But it’s an interesting development, and something to watch if the Yanks advance deeper in October.
Again, Judge isn’t in the Yankees’ first-round playoff plans due to a calf strain that might cast him as doubtful to return this year.
Stanton’s finest moments as a Yankee have come during postseason, which adds to his intrigue; as a looming option, he’d at least give an opposing manager something else to weigh.
Advertisement
On the IL since Sept. 5, Grisham might stand a better chance at activation, given the Yanks’ lack of outfield depth.
Hard-throwing righty Carlos Lagrange is pitching at the Yanks’ Somerset camp for potential playoff roster additions, coming back from a capsular (right shoulder) strain.
Lagrange’s big arm and his potential for transitioning to an impact bullpen role was an exciting prospect for the Yanks, until his injury in late July.
As of now, “he’s in the conversation for something,’’ Boone said of Lagrange, the rookie who has yet to make a big-league appearance.
Speaking of both Stanton and Lagrange, specifically, Boone said their recent activity puts them “on the outskirts of the conversation’’ about the postseason “if nothing else.’’
Clarke Schmidt, Fernando Cruz updates
After a recent bout of biceps cramping, Clarke Schmidt’s throwing session Wednesday was “better’’ than Tuesday’s effort, per Boone.
However, “if he’s not a real viable option by (Thursday), we’ll probably go a different way,’’ Boone said of Schmidt’s diminishing chances of being on a Wild Card series roster.
Though apparently minor, this is Schmidt’s second setback since his rehab from Tommy John surgery in July 2025.
Meanwhile, right-hander Fernando Cruz (partial torn UCL) threw a bullpen session Sunday, and plans to throw again Thursday.
Cruz opted against surgery and is trying to be a postseason bullpen option.
“That’s what we’re shooting for…to be back in the next couple of weeks,’’ said Cruz, adding that, in his mind, he’s not dealing with a partial tear.
“I’m going through inflammation and real chronic irritation,’’ said Cruz, determined to pitch through his condition.
Anthony Volpe will get a look at third base
Over these next few games, Boone plans to give Anthony Volpe some playing time a third base.
It's a position he's played briefly in the minors but never in the majors, though Volpe says he feels "pretty comfortable'' in his limited experience at the hot corner.
Volpe has so far made a successful transition from shortstop to second base, and "I'll just try to be prepared'' for whatever the team needs from him defensively.

Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK – La noticia sobre el regreso de Aaron Judge a la lista de lesionados aún estaba fresca, habiendo sido anunciada menos de una hora antes, y ya Cody Bellinger estaba imaginando cómo los Yankees podían tener éxito en la postemporada sin su capitán.
Desafortunadamente para Judge y su club, han tenido mucha práctica haciendo exactamente eso esta temporada. No han tenido otra opción.
"Falta Judge y duele", dijo Bellinger. "Todos sabemos que él es el mejor bateador del juego. Para nosotros aquí, nuestra mentalidad es que vamos a tener que encontrar la manera. Creo que el talento en este clubhouse habla por sí mismo. Estoy completamente seguro de que tenemos suficiente talento aquí para salir, ganar y vencer a cualquiera.
Ahora tendrán su oportunidad para demostrarlo.
El manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, confirmó el martes que Judge está lidiando con un esguince "moderado" de la pantorrilla derecha y no se espera que esté listo para una posible Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana contra los Medias Rojas, que comenzaría el 29 de septiembre.
La disponibilidad de Judge para las rondas posteriores, especialmente la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, también está en duda. Pero los Yankees necesitan llegar allí primero. Aquí hay cinco motivos por los que los Yankees, elogiados como favoritos para ganar el banderín, aún pueden llegar a la Serie Mundial incluso si Judge no regresa:
Lanzadores abridores dominantes
**
Cuando Carlos Rodón lanzó ocho entradas sin permitir carreras en la **victoria por 2-0 del martes sobre los Rays, no sólo mantuvo el champán en el clubhouse de Tampa Bay (por el momento), sino que también sirvió como un recordatorio de la mayor fortaleza de los Yankees.
Rodón podría ni siquiera abrir un partido en una posible Serie de Comodines, quedando detrás de los favoritos al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole y Max Fried. En pocas palabras, la rotación los ha mantenido a flote.
Los abridores de los Yankees han permitido dos carreras limpias o menos en 40 de 51 aperturas desde el 28 de julio, incluyendo una carrera limpia o menos en 33 de esas aperturas, acumulando efectividad de 2.50 en ese período. En general, han permitido una carrera o menos en 65 encuentros, un récord de franquicia en una sola campaña.
"Venimos a ganar cada partido, sin importar quién esté en el terreno", dijo Rodón. "Obviamente, es difícil cuando no tienes al mejor jugador del mundo en el terreno contigo. Tengo la esperanza de que vuelva. Pero... se trata simplemente de ganar juegos para nosotros.
Hay otro trueno
Esto no es el 2022, cuando los 62 jonrones de Judge establecieron un récord de la Liga Americana para una sola temporada y sirvieron como el motor indiscutible de la ofensiva. Principalmente debido a la lesión en la costilla, Judge se limitó a un promedio de .241, 18 vuelacercas y 41 impulsadas en 66 encuentros. Ben Rice asumió gran parte de la carga este año, cumpliendo con la predicción de la primavera de Boone de 39 cuadrangulares.
Bellinger sigue siendo una fuerza impactante, mientras que el aumento de la velocidad del bate del dominicano Luis García Jr. sugiere que su producción es sostenible, a pesar de una reciente caída. Mientras tanto, el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos ha mostrado poder después de un comienzo lento y se confiará en él en los playoffs contra lanzadores zurdos.
"Sabemos que somos capaces de ganar partidos", dijo Boone, quien señaló el récord de 36-24 del club desde el descanso del Juego de las Estrellas, la mayor parte del cual ocurrió sin Judge. "Nos hemos tenido que enfrentar a jugar sin muchas piezas clave en diferentes momentos y durante grandes tramos de esta campaña”.
**Los jóvenes pueden dar la cara
**
El cubano-estadounidense George Lombard Jr. y Spencer Jones llamaron la atención durante la reciente serie del club contra los Diamondbacks, cuando dieron jonrones con un total combinado de 872 pies calculados por Statcast contra Corbin Burnes – potentes batazos de 424 y 448 pies, respectivamente, que sugieren que se están sintiendo más cómodos en Grandes Ligas.
Ha habido algunos obstáculos durante sus primeros meses de actividad en las Mayores, con Lombard cometiendo errores en seis compromisos consecutivos en un período y Jones mostrando los swings en blanco que probablemente siempre sean parte de su juego. Pero el talento es real y nadie debería sorprenderse si alguno de los novatos brilla en un gran momento de octubre.
"Realmente sólo tenemos que jugar uno para el otro; apoyarnos mutuamente, pasar la batuta", dijo Bellinger. "Haces tu trabajo y controlas lo que puedes”.
Mejorando la salud
Mientras la situación de Judge no está clara, los Yankees están volviendo lentamente a estar completos.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. fue activado de la lista de lesionados entre los juego de la doble-jornada del martes, restaurando una presencia dinámica. Ha sido un año decepcionante en general, pero Chisholm estaba en racha en el momento de su lesión (de 46-18, .391). Los Yankees esperarán que retome eso.
Mientras tanto, Anthony Volpe aprovechó al máximo una oportunidad ante la ausencia de Chisholm, lo que podría haberle valido un lugar en el roster de playoffs, especialmente si los Yankees optan por contar con 11 lanzadores y 15 jugadores de posición en la primera ronda. Se cree que Trent Grisham está en la contienda para el roster.
"Con suerte, más personas podrán unirse y hacernos más formidables en el camino", dijo Boone.
Un bullpen reforzado
Los relevistas de los Yankees han estado entre los mejores de Grandes Ligas todo el año, pero ha habido señales preocupantes últimamente. Brent Headrick ocupa el segundo lugar en las Grandes Ligas con 79 presentaciones y ha mostrado una velocidad inconsistente. Mientras tanto, David Bednar y Paul Blackburn siguen en buena forma.
Debido a que los Yankees no tendrían por qué para a tener cinco abridores en octubre, la ayuda está en camino. Will Warren tiene programada una última apertura y luego pasará a un rol de relevista, dando al bullpen una opción intrigante de múltiples entradas. Clarke Schmidt y Ryan Weathers también están en consideración.
"Eso es lo bueno de la postemporada; los muchachos caen en diferentes roles y muchas veces pueden ser heroicos en papeles que no necesariamente imaginabas al inicio de la temporada", expresó Boone.

item.content:encoded:
Against Tampa Bay, Carlos Rodon gave the Yankees eight scoreless innings with eight strikeouts. That was about as much as a starter can give them against the team that has been keeping them out of first place.
They beat Tampa Bay 2-0 in the first game of Tuesday’s doubleheader. A few hours later, the Rays won 6-1 and clinched the AL East in the Bronx. Both results matter. Rodon’s start showed what this rotation can do in a playoff game; the loss showed why one excellent arm won’t settle the rest of the Yankees’ problems.
There was nothing cheap about those eight innings. Rodon kept Tampa Bay off the board long enough for Cody Bellinger’s two-run homer to stand as the entire margin. David Bednar handled the ninth. For a staff that has spent the year sorting through injuries and changing roles, that is a useful October blueprint.
The Yankees have a real decision behind their ace
Rodon’s 2.67 ERA after the first game is strong enough to make his postseason role a serious conversation. Cam Schlittler has earned the ace label, and Max Fried is still part of the picture. The question is how the Yankees order those starts and what they ask from each pitcher if the Wild Card Series arrives on schedule.
Clarke Schmidt’s return makes that decision more crowded. The rotation questions are already on the table, and Rodon just made his case with the most useful kind of outing: a long one against a division rival.
Rodon also saved the bullpen in the opener. That gets lost when the second game ends with a division celebration in the other clubhouse, but it matters if the Yankees have to play three high-pressure games in five days.
The AL East result still stings
The Yankees are in the postseason. The division title and its first-round bye belong to Tampa Bay, though, and Tuesday made the gap feel obvious. New York scored three runs in two games while its pitchers needed to be close to perfect just to force a split.
Rodon’s outing belongs in any serious October plan. It cannot cover for another quiet night from the lineup. The Yankees got a strong answer from one starter and a reminder that their hitters have less room for silence now.

NEW YORK – The news about Aaron Judge’s return to the injured list was still fresh, having been announced less than an hour earlier, and already Cody Bellinger was envisioning how the Yankees could succeed in the postseason without their captain.
Unfortunately for Judge and his club, they’ve had plenty of practice doing exactly that this season. They’ve had no choice.
“Missing Judge, it hurts,” Bellinger said. “We all know he’s the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we’re going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I’m fully confident that we have enough talent in here to go out, win and beat anybody.”
Now they’ll have their chance to prove it.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said Tuesday that Judge is dealing with a “moderate” strain of his right calf and is not expected to be ready for a potential American League Wild Card Series against the Red Sox, which would begin on Sept. 29.
Judge’s availability for subsequent rounds, especially the AL Division Series, is also in doubt. But the Yankees need to get there first. Here are five reasons why the Yankees, lauded as pennant favorites, still can reach the Fall Classic even if Judge doesn’t return:
Dominant starting pitching
Rodón might not even draw a start in a potential Wild Card Series, standing in line behind AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole and Max Fried. Simply put, the rotation has kept them afloat.
Yankees starters have permitted two earned runs or fewer in 40 of 51 starts since July 28, including one earned run or fewer in 33 of those starts, compiling a 2.50 ERA over that span. Overall, they’ve allowed one run or fewer in 65 games, a single-season franchise record.
“We come to win every game, regardless of who is on the field,” Rodón said. “Obviously it’s tough when you don’t have the best player in the world on the field with you. I’m hopeful that he’ll be back. But … it’s just about winning games for us.”
There’s other thump
This isn’t 2022, when Judge’s 62 home runs set a single-season AL record and served as the unquestioned engine of the offense. Mostly because of the rib injury, Judge was limited to a .241 average, 18 homers and 41 RBIs across 66 games. Ben Rice shouldered much of the load, fulfilling Boone’s spring prediction of 39 homers.
Bellinger remains an impactful force, while Luis García Jr.’s increased bat speed suggests his production is sustainable despite a recent slump. Meanwhile, Heliot Ramos has shown power after a sluggish start and will be leaned upon in the playoffs against left-handed pitching.
“We know we’re capable of winning games,” said Boone, who noted the club’s 36-24 record since the All-Star break, most of which occurred without Judge. “We’ve had to play without a lot of key pieces at different points and for large chunks of this season.”
The kids are all right
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones opened eyes during the club’s recent series against the Diamondbacks, when they crushed a Statcast-calculated combined 872 feet of home runs against Corbin Burnes – big-boy blasts of 424 and 448 feet, respectively, that suggested they’re growing more comfortable in The Show.
There have been growing pains across their first months of big league activity, with Lombard committing errors in six consecutive games over one span and Jones showing the swing-and-miss that will probably always be part of his game. But the talent is real, and no one should be surprised if either rookie delivers in a big October moment.
“We really just have to play for each other; lean on each other, pass the baton,” Bellinger said. “You do your job and control what you can.”
Improving health
While Judge’s outlook is cloudy, the Yankees are slowly becoming more whole.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. was activated from the injured list between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader, restoring a dynamic presence. It has been a disappointing year overall, but Chisholm was hot at the time of his injury (18-for-46, .391). The Yanks will look for him to pick up where he left off.
Meanwhile, Anthony Volpe made the most of an opportunity in Chisholm’s absence, which could have earned him a spot on a playoff roster – especially if they go with 11 pitchers and 15 position players in the first round. Trent Grisham is thought to be in play for the playoff roster.
“Hopefully more people are able to join and make us more formidable along the way,” Boone said.
A bolstered bullpen
The Yankees’ relievers have been among the league’s best all year, but there have been concerning signs of late. Brent Headrick ranks second in the Majors with 79 appearances and has seen inconsistent velocity, for example, suggesting he could benefit from a breather once the AL East is decided. David Bednar and Paul Blackburn, meanwhile, remain sharp.
Because the Yankees would have no reason to roster five starting pitchers in October, help is on the way. Will Warren is scheduled to make one more start and then transition to a relief role, giving the ’pen an intriguing multi-inning option. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are also in the mix.
“That’s the beauty of the postseason; guys fall into different roles and a lot of times can become heroic in roles you didn’t necessarily count on at the start of the season,” Boone said.

Chisholm’s most memorable moment, though, was failing to cover first base on a safety squeeze in the 6-1 loss in The Bronx that helped the Rays clinch the division.
With one out and runners on the corners in the seventh inning and Taylor Walls at the plate, manager Aaron Boone said the Yankees were aware that a bunt would be coming “more often than not.”
And sure enough, Walls pushed a bunt toward first base, and Luis García Jr. charged, as he was supposed to, Boone said.
Chisholm started to run over but stopped, believing García would halt his charge and return to the base. Chisholm instead hovered by second base.
“He’s just gotta go [to first base] every time, and he knows that,” Boone said of Chisholm, who acknowledged the mistake.
“Next time, I’ll just keep going through,” said Chisholm, who was sidelined for two weeks after spraining his right thumb Sept. 8 and has returned to a team sorting out its infield with five games to go before the postseason.
Asked before the doubleheader if Volpe would continue to get time at second with Chisholm back, Boone said, “We’ll see.”
Chisholm went 1-for-3 with a single and a walk, while Volpe went 0-for-3 with three strikeouts in the 2-0 doubleheader opener. Entering play, Volpe had hit .286 with a .753 OPS in 10 games with Chisholm on the IL.
The Yankees also have to figure out third base, as Ryan McMahon is a mess on both sides of the ball.
José Caballero got the start there in the opener against Martinez and went 1-for-3 with a pair of stolen bases, with lefty-swinging McMahon in the lineup for the nightcap against Drew Rasmussen. Amed Rosario, signed in the offseason with the idea of playing third against lefties, has not produced in those situations this year, and the Yankees have mostly gone with Caballero and McMahon over the last three weeks.

Another source said an IL stint isn’t out of the question as Schmidt is trying to earn a spot on the postseason roster after missing over a year following Tommy John surgery.
Ryan Weathers threw a bullpen session between games as he works to return from a left forearm strain, and Fernando Cruz (UCL) played catch.

item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

The Yankees activated Clarke Schmidt from the 60-day injured list on Sept. 16. On paper, that should read like uncomplicated good news. In late September, it really is another decision sitting on the manager’s desk.
Clarke Schmidt has logged just two-thirds of an inning in 2026. He is active, but he has not had the time to rebuild a normal starter’s workload while Carlos Rodon, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are already taking up the big innings.
Add Will Warren to that conversation and the Yankees have more options than clean answers. A talented pitcher returning late is useful. It can also make the October board much harder to read.
The Yankees cannot let sentiment choose the role
Schmidt earned real trust before the injury, which makes this harder than it would be for a fringe arm. He is not someone the Yankees should stash in the background and forget about.
But a postseason roster does not care about last spring or last year. It cares about who can get through a difficult inning right now. The Yankees need to decide whether Schmidt can help as a short reliever, a piggyback option or simply depth behind their first group of starters.
The answer does not have to be permanent this week. It does need to be honest. Trying to force a long starter’s buildup into the final days of the season would create a problem the Yankees do not need.
October will reward the Yankees for getting practical
Schmidt returning gives the Yankees an extra good pitcher. That matters. The club should enjoy having more pitching than most teams can claim this late in the year.
Still, the safest route is probably the simplest one: use him in the role his current workload supports, then see if the games demand more. The Yankees have enough established starters. What they need from Schmidt is clarity, not a rushed label.

A flurry of injury news came across for the battered and bruised Bronx Bombers on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium.
While the team is clearly compromised and will likely be missing their best player, Aaron Judge, when the playoffs start on Sept. 29, they will be getting their second baseman back with some time to get ready for the inevitable Wild Card Series vs. the Boston Red Sox.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. is expected to be activated between games on Tuesday as the Bombers begin their four-game set with the Tampa Bay Rays with a day-night doubleheader. Chisholm Jr. has been out since Sept. 8 with a right thumb sprain.
“He should be in a good spot and ready to go,” said manager Aaron Boone. “He’s been hitting now for several days and and throwing the last three or four days, so he should be ready to go.”
The 28-year-old is slashing .232/.312/.403 with 19 homers and 55 RBI in 134 games this season. The impending free agent is expected to resume duties as their starting second baseman, which likely doesn’t bode well for Anthony Volpe’s playing time.
“Obviously, Anthony’s done a good job,” said Boone. “But looking forward to getting Jazz back as well. So, Jazz, I plan on playing Jazz at second in the night game.”
Volpe has performed well since being recalled from Triple-A on Sept. 10, slashing .286/.324/.429 with a homer, seven RBI and four stolen bases. It remains to be seen how he will be utilized and if a platoon scenario between Volpe and Chisholm Jr. is on the table.
CLARKE GOOD
Clarke Schmidt appears to have avoided anything major after experiencing bicep soreness while warming up during Sunday’s loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks.
“Clark is gonna play catch [Tuesday]. He did have some testing and it looks like he’s in a pretty good spot.” Boone said. “But [he’s] gotta throw and see how he is, and then we’ll go from there. … He’s on the active roster for now, but he’s got to play catch and do all those things and see how available he is.”
Schmidt returned from Tommy John surgery on Sept. 16 against the Minnesota Twins. He is expected to play a crucial role out of the bullpen in whatever time the Yankees have in the postseason.
WEATHERS UPDATE
Ryan Weathers (left forearm flexor strain) will throw a side session between games on Tuesday. Weathers exited his start against the Toronto Blue Jays on Aug 22 after feeling discomfort and has not appeared in a game since.
If the southpaw is to return in the postseason, it will very likely be out of the bullpen.

NUEVA YORK -- Aaron Judge tiene una distensión de “grado moderado” en la pantorrilla derecha y probablemente se pierda al menos el inicio de la postemporada de los Yankees, según el manager Aaron Boone, quien dijo que el club no planea tener a su capitán activo para una posible Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana contra los Medias Rojas.
“Estamos planeando que no sea parte de eso”, dijo Boone el martes. “Pero también estamos en una época del año en la que... obviamente lo forzaríamos un poco si eso estuviera en juego. Pero falta una semana para eso. No lo espero, pero tampoco lo descarto”.
Los Yankees han asegurado un pase a la postemporada, pero los Rays pueden amarrar el título del Este de la Liga Americana y el sembrado Nro. 1 de la L.A. con una victoria en cualquiera de los choques de la doble cartelera del martes, lo que obligaría a Nueva York a disputar la Serie del Comodín.
Judge fue ingresado a la lista de lesionados de 10 días el sábado, retroactivo al 17 de septiembre.
Recibió una inyección de plasma pobre en plaquetas en la pantorrilla derecha durante el día libre del lunes y tendrá actividades limitadas durante los próximos días.
“El par de días siguientes no habrá mucho: nada de correr, saltar, cosas así”, indicó Boone.
Durante la serie del club el fin de semana en Phoenix, Judge y Boone fueron vagos sobre la gravedad de la lesión, la cual Judge sufrió durante la serie de la semana pasada frente a los Mellizos.
Judge reveló que la distensión es en el músculo sóleo de su pantorrilla derecha, el cual dijo “es un poco más crucial al correr y batear”.
“He lidiado con distensiones antes y de alguna manera he jugado con ellas, pero esta fue en un lugar diferente donde lo hizo un poco más difícil”, comentó Judge.
Generalmente, una distensión de pantorrilla de Grado 2 toma de tres a seis semanas para recuperarse.
“Si él es capaz de jugar, entonces le daremos esa oportunidad”, señaló Boone.
Judge se perdió la mayor parte del verano con una fractura en la costilla derecha, que se cree sufrió el 26 de abril en Houston. Jugó con la lesión antes de ingresar a la lista de lesionados a principios de junio.
Activado en septiembre sin una asignación de rehabilitación en liga menor, Judge disputó sólo siete compromisos después de ser activado, bateando de 23-4 (.174) con un jonrón. En general, Judge bateó .241/.360/.511 con 18 bambinazos y 41 carreras impulsadas en 66 partidos esta campaña.
“Hemos jugado gran parte del año sin él, y en su mayor parte, hemos hecho un trabajo bastante bueno”, destacó Boone. “Obviamente, siempre quieres a tu mejor jugador disponible. Pero entendemos que tenemos un trabajo que hacer y una expectativa de ganar. Creo que esa expectativa no cambia, con o sin él”.
En otras actualizaciones de lesiones, Boone dijo que los Yankees tienen la intención de activar al infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr. entre los encuentros de la doble cartelera del martes.
El derecho Clarke Schmidt se sometió a estudios de imagen tras necesitar acortar su calentamiento el domingo en Phoenix debido a una molestia en su bíceps derecho.
“Por ahora está en el roster activo, pero tiene que soltar el brazo y hacer todas esas cosas para ver qué tan disponible está”, declaró Boone.

item.content:encoded:
It's funny to think that at one point it felt like sacrilege to even consider trading Luis Gil for anyone. Here was the prospective American League Rookie of the Year who held it down in the rotation while Gerrit Cole was sidelined for much of 2024, and the Houston Astros wanted him as the centerpiece of a trade for Kyle Tucker. The New York Yankees scoffed at the idea and opted to keep Gil.
In hindsight, they should have landed Tucker and sent Gil to Houston. Gil immediately broke down, and his velocity has never been what it was during his first full season, when he earned rookie honors. It's a trade they likely would have won even if Tucker ended up still going to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
That one successful year feels like a lifetime ago, but now the Yankees have a chance to salvage some of his value. With injuries to Ryan Weathers, a Clarke Schmidt scare this past week, and Brent Headrick's velocity alarmingly down over the weekend, the bullpen is looking shaky heading into the postseason. With just a week left in the regular season, they should use this opportunity to see what they have in Gil.
In the best-case scenario, Gil would be relegated to lower-leverage situations. That is how they have used him, too. Gil has seen just five appearances over the last month, but things feel a little more dire, and Boone used him twice in their most recent series against the Arizona Diamondbacks. It could be a signal that they're giving Gil one last chance to prove himself. There might not be another choice, either.
The best use of Gil moving forward
Call it a bit of a Hail Mary, but it wouldn't hurt the Yankees at this point if they used Gil in medium- to high-leverage situations against the Tampa Bay Rays and Baltimore Orioles. If he can hack it, at least they know what they have. The same goes if he fails there. At least they know not to use him in that role in the postseason.
Better to find out now, when the games don't matter and the postseason is already set. Chances are the Rays aren't losing the next seven games and blowing the division, either.
One thing about Gil is that his velocity looks like it's up. He averaged 95.4 MPH on his fastball this season. Since being called up on August 31st, Gil has averaged 96.1 MPH. His slider velocity is up as well. He's averaging 87.1 MPH on it since the call-up. He is sitting at 85.8 MPH this season.
Gil's strikeout numbers are also slightly up in this small sample size. Since his call-up, he has pitched six innings and struck out eight with just three walks. He has allowed one earned run, but that was back in his first start.
Another thing about Gil is that the Yankees are waiting for his arm to return to what it used to be. He may never be what he once was, and with a stacked rotation, his only role as a Yankee is likely in the bullpen. That said, this final week could be one of Gil's most important.
It's an opportunity to show that he still has some value to the team, and if he's able to get outs, blowing heaters by batters this week and into the postseason, they don't have to feel all that bad about watching Tucker go elsewhere in 2025 — not that it would have mattered in the long run anyway.

Yankees' playoff picture, Aaron Judge update and potential rotation
This wasn’t how the Yankees wanted to move into the regular season’s final week, with a four-game set against Tampa Bay.
Beginning with Tuesday’s day-night doubleheader, they’ll need to sweep the AL East leaders just to prevent the Rays from spilling champagne inside Yankee Stadium’s visiting clubhouse.
And there’s uncertainty surrounding Yankees captain Aaron Judge’s availability next week – the start of postseason − due to a right calf strain.
“We’ve been through a lot as a team this year already and we’ve answered the bell at mostly all the turns,’’ Yanks manager Aaron Boone told reporters, including the YES Network, after Sunday’s 8-4 loss at Arizona.
“(We’re) looking forward to hopefully playing a good week of baseball and building some momentum going into the postseason.’’
Here’s a look at the Yankees’ week ahead:
Yankees vs Rays with AL East race nearing its end
In winning 12 of their last 15 games, the Rays (95-60) have opened a six-game divisional lead on the Yanks (89-66).
On the verge of its first AL East title since 2021, Tampa Bay could clinch it with one win on a long Tuesday in the Bronx.
Tuesday’s opener has Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-4, 2.94) scheduled to oppose lefty Carlos Rodon (6-3, 2.95), with righty Drew Rasmussen (15-5, 2.72) vs. lefty Max Fried (5-4, 2.63) in the nightcap.
The Yanks are scheduled to start Gerrit Cole on Wednesday and Cam Schlittler on Thursday.
In the wider picture, Boone acknowledged the need to prep for next week, which includes giving important bullpen arms like Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn some added rest.
“You’ve got to make sure guys are in a good spot going in (to postseason),’’ Boone told reporters, speaking generally on Sunday.
“But we’re going to show up and try to win the games on Tuesday.’’
Aaron Judge injury update
Judge’s availability for the first playoff round remains a mystery.
This past weekend, Judge told reporters: “I’d like to be back by the postseason. That’s definitely the plan.’’
Judge said he’s played through minor calf strains before, but this current injury to the soleus muscle is a more problematic spot.
So, this will be a key week of treatment and testing to see if Judge could be available in any capacity for a first-round playoff series.
Yankees injury news as Jazz Chisholm Jr. might return
Sidelined since Sept. 9, lefty-hitting second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. (right thumb sprain) could be activated from the injured list to start the Tampa Bay series.
Though he’s unlikely to be activated this week, lefty reliever Ryan Weathers (flexor strain) could find himself on a playoff roster next week in a bullpen capacity.
On the IL since Sept. 5, center fielder Trent Grisham (strained right hamstring) has progressed in his running and is also a possible postseason choice.
Recovered from Tommy John surgery rehab, right-hander Clarke Schmidt developed cramping in his right biceps area while warming up Sunday.
Schmidt did not enter the game, telling reporters it was “more precautionary…especially with the playoffs coming up,’’ in what could be an important relief role.
Initial testing revealed no shoulder or elbow issues, but Schmidt planned to be examined by the team physician Monday.
Schmidt called it “frustrating,’’ but feels “in the grand scheme, we’ll be out there soon.’’
How Yankees' playoff rotation might look
With the likelihood of the Yanks hosting a best-of-three Wild Card series beginning Tuesday, they'd have Cam Schlittler ready on regular rest vs. Boston in Game 1.
But that might not be how the Yankees set things up.
Gerrit Cole would be on one extra day of rest if he's the Game 1 choice, or the Yanks could give the ball to Max Fried with nearly a full week of rest. It's been one month since Fried's return from a second elbow bone bruise this season.
Carlos Rodon could be on a Wild Card roster in an emergency or long relief capacity, or he might be saved to start Game 1 or 2 of a best-of-five Division Series.
CC Sabathia to be honored at Yankee Stadium
Prior to Saturday night's game against the Orioles, CC Sabathia's No. 52 will be retired in a ceremony at Yankee Stadium.
He'll be the 24th Yankees player or manager so honored and the first since Paul O'Neill, who had his No. 21 retired in August 2022.

After Chisholm got hurt diving into second base Sept. 8, the Yankees called up Anthony Volpe to get some run at the position he had mostly transitioned to at Triple-A, and he made the most of it.
In the 10 games since Volpe was recalled, he has started at second base nine times (José Caballero started the other) and mostly looked sharp, batting .286 with a .753 OPS and four steals.
Whether Volpe has done enough to warrant at-bats once Chisholm returns remains to be seen. Shortly before he was called back up, the natural shortstop had also started to mix in some third base, starting three games there, though Aaron Boone would only offer, “We’ll see,” when asked whether that could be an option for Volpe with Chisholm back.
“First things first, getting Jazz back and then we’ll figure it out as the week unfolds how I want to play it,” Boone said.
The Yankees have not gotten much offensive production from their third basemen this year, especially of late. Since returning from his own thumb sprain Sept. 1, Ryan McMahon has hit just 6-for-40 (.150) with a .402 OPS, with Caballero starting at third over him Sunday against a righty. Amed Rosario has often started at third against lefties, and while he has not hit in line with his career numbers, the Yankees continue to believe he will.
Boone could also platoon Volpe and Chisholm at second base, as the lefty-hitting Chisholm is batting only .221 with a .654 OPS against lefties. But the pending free agent had just been starting to get hot in a disappointing season, hitting .391 with a 1.028 OPS over his last 15 games before getting hurt.
If and where Volpe fits on the playoff roster is just one of the many decisions they will have to consider over this final week of the regular season.
“You know it’s going to take a lot of players and a lot of people when you get to spring training and the season unfolds,” Boone said. “We’ll have hopefully some tough decisions to make when we’re setting postseason rosters and things like that. But that’s a better problem to have.”

The New York Yankees opted not to add any relief pitchers at the MLB trade deadline. Why? Because Ryan Weathers was going to end up in the bullpen, and Clarke Schmidt was due to return.
The Yankees were relying on two pitchers with extensive injury histories to solidify their bullpen in October. What could possibly go wrong?
Well, everything that could have gone wrong has gone wrong for New York.
Weathers suffered an elbow flexor strain last month and has been sidelined ever since. It now doesn't appear that the left-hander will return before the playoffs, leaving his postseason status in jeopardy.
Schmidt? He suffered a setback at the beginning of August due to forearm cramping. He then finally returned last week and pitched all of one game before ultimately succumbing to biceps cramping while warming up in the bullpen over the weekend.
Naturally, New York ruled him out for the contest.
Schmidt said it was precautionary and that he didn't want to push through, but are we really to think that a pitcher who had been sidelined since last summer after undergoing Tommy John surgery and had made a grand total of 30 appearances between 2024 and 2025 is going to magically rebound and be just fine?
Maybe the right-hander really is okay and will be available sooner than we think, but you can't help but feel that Schmidt's playoff status, much like that of Weathers, is now in limbo.
It make Brian Cashman's mind-boggling decision not to acquire relief help last month that much more egregious, and it moves the Yankees even further away from a deep October run, something that was probably already foreign anyway following Aaron Judge's latest trip to the injured list.
Yes, New York picked up John Schreiber on the waiver wire, and he has certainly helped, logging a 2.00 ERA over eight relief appearances. He will almost certainly be on the postseason roster.
But Schreiber alone isn't enough. Not with Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn burning the candle from both ends and Tim Hill turning into a batting practice machine.
Had Weathers and Schmidt remained healthy, there's no question they would have been able to help. It's the fact that Cashman was whimsically relying on it that's so nonsensical.
I've been a big Cashman defender over the years. I think he's been a very good general manager for a long time. But it's becoming harder and harder to defend his decisions.
Just about every other contending team acquired bullpen help at the trade deadline. Apparently, the Yankees were the only ballclub too good to do so.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- Varias latas de cerveza fueron vaciadas sobre la cabeza de Aaron Judge mientras el capitán de los Yankees permanecía en el centro del clubhouse de visitantes en el Target Field la semana pasada, rodeado de compañeros eufóricos que celebraban la clasificación del club a la postemporada.
Judge entrecerró los ojos por el ardor y les advirtió a sus compañeros: “Me las van a pagar”.
Aun así, no pretenden que ésa sea su última celebración, pues tienen un firme control del primer puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana y el título del Este de la Liga Americana todavía está en juego.
“Siempre es bueno cuando puedes celebrar esos momentos durante una temporada”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. “Mucha gente dedica mucho tiempo, esfuerzo y sudor. Obviamente, éste es apenas el primer paso de lo que esperamos sean muchos”.
Ahora que aseguraron su pase a la postemporada, ¿qué más les espera a los Yankees?
¿Cómo podría quedar el roster para la postemporada?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez 
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos
BD: Ben Rice
LA: Gerrit Cole, Cam Schlittler, Max Fried
R: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber, Will Warren, Carlos Rodón
Los Yankees utilizaron a 12 lanzadores y a 14 bateadores cuando recibieron a los Medias Rojas en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, así que partiremos de esa misma premisa para el 2026.
Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles contra Tampa Bay, mientras que Schlittler lo hará el jueves. Mirando hacia adelante, eso sugiere que Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Es posible que los Yankees estén alineando a Cole para abrir el Juego 1 y a Schlittler para el Juego 2. Hasta ahora, han preferido no decir mucho al respecto, salvo por la confirmación de Boone de que Cole realizará una apertura en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Rodón podría estar en el bullpen para la serie. En nuestra proyección del roster lo tenemos activo, mientras que el dominicano Luis Gil y Ryan Yarbrough figuran entre quienes quedarían fuera. Ryan Weathers trabaja para regresar como relevista, pero el tiempo juega en su contra. Si está saludable, podría ocupar el lugar de Fulmer o Schreiber.
Chisholm espera regresar esta semana para la serie contra los Rays tras sufrir un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Grisham ha mostrado mejoría y podría quedarse con un puesto en los jardines. De no ser así, Max Schuemann está entre las alternativas. Otro aspecto para seguir: ¿Podrían los Yankees incluir a Anthony Volpe en lugar de Rosario? Es una posibilidad que vale la pena considerar.
¿Cuándo comenzará la postemporada?
Si los Yankees terminan disputando la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, ésta empezará el 29 de septiembre. La Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana arrancará el 3 de octubre.
¿Contra quién jugarían los Yankees si la temporada terminara hoy?
En estos momentos, sería una revancha de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, con los Yankees recibiendo a los Medias Rojas en el Bronx. Los Yankees ganaron aquella serie dos victorias por una.
Este año, los Yankees tuvieron marca de 7-6 contra Boston.
¿Todavía pueden ganar el Este de la Liga Americana?
Sí, pero tienen un camino cuesta arriba. Los Yankees tienen por delante cuatro enfrentamientos directos con los Rays a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium, incluyendo una doble-cartelera para abrir la serie. Tampa Bay domina actualmente la serie particular por 6-3, lo que significa que los Yankees necesitarían barrer para quedarse con el criterio de desempate entre ambos.
¿Quién abriría el Juego 1 por los Yankees?
Como se mencionó anteriormente, Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles frente a Tampa Bay y Schlittler lo hará al día siguiente. Por lo tanto, Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Después de permitir siete jonrones en sus dos aperturas anteriores, Cole mermó las dudas externas sobre una posible apertura en los playoffs con una sólida actuación en Arizona. Fried y Rodón han lidiado con lesiones, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado.
Warren realizará una apertura más durante la serie contra los Orioles, según Boone, pero llegará a los playoffs como una interesante alternativa para el relevo.
¿Será Judge un factor en los playoffs?
Los Yankees han sido poco específicos sobre el estado de Judge. Boone ha evitado ofrecer un plazo estimado para su recuperación e incluso revelar el grado del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha. En términos generales, hasta un tirón de Grado 1, el de menor gravedad, requiere de dos a tres semanas para una recuperación completa.
Es casi seguro que Judge intentará regresar antes. La primera fecha en la que podría ser activado sería para el Juego 162, el 27 de septiembre. Tal como está el panorama ahora mismo, existe una posibilidad muy real de que los Yankees no cuenten con Judge al menos para una potencial Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Judge dijo que le “gustaría” estar activo para la postemporada y que ése es “el plan”, pero no dijo necesariamente que sería para el 29 de septiembre.
¿Cuáles son las otras preocupaciones en cuanto a lesiones?
Grisham ha avanzado en su programa progresivo de correr y debe de estar disponible para el roster de los playoffs, aunque Boone dijo que no será activado antes de que termine la temporada regular. Chisholm ha estado bateando y realizando tiros, y debe de ser activado durante la serie contra los Rays. Si sufre algún contratiempo, Volpe entraría en consideración.
Y aunque los Yankees no han descartado a Giancarlo Stanton, quien ha estado bateando, han ofrecido pocas novedades sobre su recuperación del más reciente tirón en la pantorrilla.

Clarke Schmidt downplayed the latest issue involving his right arm after the New York Yankees' 8-4 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Sunday.
Schmidt was unavailable to pitch because of biceps cramps, according to Bob Nightengale of USA TODAY. The right-hander described the decision as precautionary and is expected to see a team doctor in New York.
Schmidt does not have any diagnostic tests scheduled at this point. The update comes just four days after he returned to the Yankees following a lengthy recovery from Tommy John surgery.
Yankees pitcher Clarke Schmidt, who had biceps cramps and couldn’t come into the game, described it as precautionary.
He will see a doctor back in NY but no testing is planned
The Yankees activated Schmidt from the 60-day injured list on Sept. 16. He made his return against the Minnesota Twins, throwing two-thirds of an inning and recording two strikeouts.
Schmidt underwent surgery in July 2025 after tearing the UCL in his right elbow. The procedure kept him out for roughly 14 months and limited his time to a short late-season return.
Rather than immediately returning to the starting rotation, Schmidt was expected to work as a multi-inning reliever. The Yankees planned to manage his workload carefully while evaluating how he could contribute during the postseason.
The latest issue adds another layer of uncertainty, although Schmidt's own description suggests the team is not treating it as a major setback at this stage.
The Yankees entered Sunday with an 89-66 record and had already secured a postseason berth. They remain six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with the regular season nearing its conclusion.
Schmidt's availability could become increasingly important as New York prepares for October. For now, the Yankees will wait for his evaluation in New York before determining whether the biceps issue will affect his return to the bullpen.

More than almost any other New York Yankees playoff run, this October's edition will provide either immediate vindication for Brian Cashman's trade deadline strategy or all-new reasons to directly blame him for the team's failure. It should be fascinating to watch, if you don't actually have much emotional energy invested in the team's well-being. Clarke Schmidt's postgame note on Sunday evening was just another reason to be anxious about the way this bullpen was constructed and the amount of variables therein.
Trade deadline predictions for the Yankees' haul this year were astoundingly easy to make. A catcher, first and foremost. An impact bat, that was obvious. And then two bullpen arms to help save their late-inning core from running aground before the year ended. Maybe one would be a certified ace, a tier below Mason Miller, but still devilish. Maybe another would be a bounce back candidate or a never-was, someone who Matt Blake could unearth. Either way, the choices were many, but the outcome was obvious: CashGod would be trading for some relievers. Plural.
But then the deadline came and went. We weren't disappointed by the quality of the haul, but rather in a whole new way. No catcher? No relievers? Was this a mistake? Is the deadline tomorrow?
Nope. Cashman went all in and decided that either the prices were too high or not commensurate with the talent available. Instead, he would look the other way and ignore the rising cost of wear-and-tear in August and piece together some bullpen reinforcements using alternate levers. The waiver wire became his friend. His rotation became a plucking ground, as did his own Injured List. Will Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Weathers, Luis Gil, Will Warren, John Schreiber and Michael Fulmer be more valuable together than any names he could've added on Aug. 3? That's the bet. We'll see. I have my doubts, but he has his agenda.
And, in case you weren't already lacking confidence, Schmidt's bicep barked on Sunday and prevented him from entering the game, a game that ace reliever Brent Headrick lit on fire with an average fastball that dipped about a mile and a half below his standard velocity on the season. Hmm. If only he could've been rested during the dog days of summer.
Clarke Schmidt's worrisome postgame comments, Brent Headrick outing vs. Diamondbacks tell the same Yankees story
So, for the record, that's Schmidt - after one MLB outing this year - admitting that, out of precaution, he stopped warming up when his arm barked. His rehab was also halted along the way when he felt forearm cramping on Aug. 4, just one day post-trade deadline. The Yankees getting him back to the MLB level after a summer 2025 Tommy John surgery is remarkable. This is not someone a team should be relying on to cover meaningful postseason innings. And yet.
Headrick's stumble comes in an otherwise phenomenal year, and even as he's lost some gas down the stretch, he's still managed to mostly make things work. He's an expert at limiting inherited runners from scoring, and he's alternated spotless outings with troublesome ones post-deadline. No one knows for certain whether bringing on an experienced seventh-inning guy or two in early August would've prevented the effects of overuse from piling up on Headrick's left arm, but we do know having a viable alternative now could help them deemphasize Headrick if he's struggling to recapture his former glory. Batters hit .345 off him in 15 August games.
That group of alternatives probably doesn't, or shouldn't, include Schmidt, who's hanging on by a thread. Again, it'll be Cashman's crew - Schreiber, Fulmer, Warren, and maybe Weathers, who won't be rehabbing in a regular season game - vs. the field to see who's better equipped for October. Fascinating, if it weren't so presumptuous.
